segs.text: From 1923 until his death in 1951, one man in southern Florida cut, moved and stood up stone blocks that weigh many tons each. His name was Edward Leedskalnin. The castle's own figure for the total is about eleven hundred tons. Here is what is documented, what he claimed, what people have guessed, and what is still unknown.

Start with the man. Edward Leedskalnin was born in Latvia in 1887. A 1984 National Register nomination form says that at about twenty-six he was engaged to a girl ten years younger, Agnes, who called off the wedding shortly before it. The form says he later called her his Sweet Sixteen. After years of work across North America and illness, he reached Florida City in the early 1920s.
Even that part has gaps. Her surname appears as Scuff and Skuvst, and one Latvian account gives a different name and age. Why he built it comes from later tellings: the story as told, not a record.

In 1923, according to the form, he bought one acre near Florida City for twelve dollars. The ground was oolitic limestone, popularly called coral rock. He built a shed, then a two story tower, a wall, and carved furniture and astronomy pieces from the rock around him.

In the mid nineteen thirties he bought ten acres in Homestead, about ten miles north, and decided to take his stone with him. The dates conflict. The form says 1937. The obelisk is inscribed: moved in 1939, and the castle's own chronology says land clearing began in May 1939. A farmer, Bob Biggers, hauled the stones. Accounts say Ed loaded and unloaded them himself, at night.

Now the weights, as printed in the 1984 form, in pounds. The Polaris sighting slab: twenty short tons. Each quarter moon: eighteen. The full moon fountain: twenty three. The obelisk: twenty eight and a half. The heaviest it names: thirty tons. The castle's own site says over twenty one. These are published estimates, not weighings.

What about the famous total, eleven hundred tons? It appears on the castle's website and in encyclopedias with no named estimator; the 1984 form gives none. The earliest number we found is over a thousand tons, in a 1950s book by the engineer Carrol Lake. We could not find where eleven hundred first appears. So: a claim, source untraced.

The best known piece is the gate. A single slab, eighty one inches wide, ninety two tall, twenty one thick, turning on a central shaft that the form says uses an automobile axle. It was reported to turn with one finger. The form calls it nine tons. Accounts say it stopped turning in the mid nineteen eighties, 1984 or 1986. Six men and a crane lifted it out, and a rusted truck bearing was replaced.

Here is a check anyone can do. Those dimensions come to about ninety cubic feet. Even if the whole rectangle were solid aragonite, it would weigh about eight tons. Real oolite is porous; at an assumed thirty percent, nearer five and a half. So nine tons is probably a rounded figure. Five tons on one finger is still remarkable.

What tools did he have? The form lists his tools, made partly from old car parts: block and tackle, rollers, jacks, wedges, slings, cables, sledges and chisels. Old photographs show tall wooden tripods with chains, and a chain hoist. An independent archive says no detailed record shows how the rigs were used.

What can that gear do? Take a ten ton block, twenty thousand pounds. A block and tackle with six rope segments cuts the pull to a sixth: about thirty three hundred pounds. Chain two sets together and it is six times six: about five hundred fifty. Add a five to one winch and it is near one hundred ten pounds. The price is distance: the tackle rope moves thirty six feet per foot of lift, and the winch handle about one hundred eighty. Small force, long time. This is ideal physics, no friction: what is possible, not what he did.

Levers work on the same idea. A bar with nine feet on one side of the pivot and one on the other multiplies your push by nine. Raise a block an inch, slide a timber under, repeat. That is the principle, not a plan for ten tons. It is slow, and needs only time.

So what is not documented? In 1955, the castle's new owner collected more than two hundred fifty signed affidavits saying Ed worked alone with simple hand tools. But the form quotes no one who watched the largest blocks go up. So the belief is documented. The method is not.

Now his own words. Asked how, the form says, Ed always answered that he understood the methods of the pyramid builders, and the laws of leverage and weight. That is a claim. We found no document where he describes his lifting method. He published pamphlets in 1936 and 1945, including Magnetic Current, on his own ideas about magnets.

Then the popular theories. Sound levitation. Magnetism, the subject of his pamphlets, though they do not say so. Help from beyond Earth, or mastered gravity, ideas the 1984 form already records. All are not established. We found no measurement, recording, or physical trace for any, and the floating stone stories are secondhand. Absence of evidence is not proof of absence. So: not established, not impossible.

So here is the ledger. Documented: the land purchase, the form's printed weights, the tool list, photographs of hoisting gear. Reported, with conflicts: the move dates, the gate repair. Claimed: that he worked alone, that he knew the pyramid builders' methods, the eleven hundred ton total. Not settled: the gate's true weight. Unknown: exactly how the largest blocks were raised and set. That he worked alone is claimed.

Patient work with simple machines fits the tools, the photographs and the physics. Fits is not the same as shown. Could something stranger be going on? Not established. Not ruled out. Someone watching this might be the one who works it out.
